title: SIU findings outrage James Foldi's family
article: LINCOLN - The family of a Beamsville man who died last summer while in police custody, is "outraged" at the conclusions of a Special Investigations Unit investigation into the incident.

Steven Foldi, whose brother James died July 1 after police shot him with a Taser gun, says his family is not pleased with the SIU's conclusion, which was expected to be released sometime this week. Foldi said he received a call from SIU Investigator John Line, Wednesday, to inform him of the findings. Foldi says the SIU has concluded that based on toxicology reports, his brother was killed as a result of the "high concentration of cocaine in his system".

The report was not available at press time, but Rose Bliss, communications spokesperson with the SIU said it is "comprehensive and detailed" and does provide a thorough explanation of the circumstances surrounding James Foldi's death based on the SIU's investigation.

The death of 39-year-old Foldi followed his arrest by Niagara Regional Police officers, after he was identified as a suspect in a number of reported break-and-enter incidents in the Village Park Drive and Crescent Avenue area of Beamsville. In the early morning hours of July 1, several homeowners reported that Foldi had smashed windows to gain entry into their homes, had been exhibiting bizarre behaviour and appeared to be under the influence of drugs. During the course of the arrest, a Taser gun was used. The zappers utilize two energy probes that conduct nearly 50,000 volts of electricity at a maximum firing range of 26-feet. The Taser can be used as a stun weapon as well, and works to disrupt the sensory and motor systems of the body.
After Foldi was taken into police custody, he was transported to West Lincoln Memorial Hospital, where he died.

The SIU investigators focused on the events leading up to his death to determine what the nature and extent of police involvement was. No details have been released in the SIU's investigation, which included interviewing witnesses, the officers involved and attending the post-mortem examination on July 2.
"We're going to challenge it," said Steven Foldi in an interview Wednesday. "There's still a lot of unanswered questions people refuse to answer for us."
One of those questions, he said, surrounds the nature of his brother's death. Foldi says the family is "puzzled".

"They're saying he overdosed, yet he left his home, apparently got in an altercation with a couple of people, and was able to run from the police," he said. "You don't run around the corner, have all the cops chasing you and get pepper sprayed and tasered if you've OD-ed."

Steven Foldi said the lack of information they have received from the SIU has also upset the family. When they initially started the investigation, he said the family asked the SIU to formally sit down with them to discuss the findings. Now, he said, they were simply called and told of the results just a day before it would be released for public consumption, a move he called "disgusting".
"We have no information on how he died, where he died. No information at all," he said.
Foldi said he would also like to know why the investigation took so long.
"If it was a simple overdose it could have taken weeks. This has gotten the family outraged," he said.

Foldi admitted the family was "quite surprised" his brother was using cocaine, saying he knew he was a "social drinker" and that he was a "family man" with four kids and a wife in a wheelchair he had been taking care of for several years.
Foldi said their father is now taking care of family.
As for what steps the family will take now, Foldi said they are ready to challenge the findings.
"We're going to take it as far as we can go. We're not satisfied with the result," he said.
Foldi says he will have to take up his appeal through the Attorney General's office. According to the SIU, however, there is no appeal process for its decisions.
"The director's decision is final," said Bliss, adding the SIU is an independent agency that operates with "no political influence" from the government or police.
Brendan Crawley, a senior coordinator of media relations in the communications branch of the Ministry of the Attorney General, confirmed Bliss' comments, saying an SIU finding is not appealable.
"The short answer is no, someone can not appeal an SIU finding," he said.
Foldi said the family is also considering civil action.
"Number one, we'd like some answers. Number two, we'd like the police to take some responsibility," he said, adding it is his understanding a public inquiry into the incident will be called.
Foldi says he was told police fired three Taser shots at his brother, but just one penetrated. He said he believes police should not have used the weapon on his brother because he was on narcotics.

In an interview with Niagara This Week in June, however, Const. Todd Blair of the Niagara Regional Police, the service's use of force instructor, said the Taser can assist with the police's approach to stopping violent suspects, sometimes those under the influence of narcotics. He said when Tasers are used, a five-second shock is fired and then police watch for a change in behaviour of the person they are trying to subdue.

Foldi also said he was not pleased his brother was tasered as he was calling out for help when police were arresting him. Neighbours home at the time of the incident also said he was calling out for help, in what one neighbour described as him going "berserk".
"These people, when they're called, are supposed to help you," said Foldi.
- with files from Joe Fantauzzi and Joanne McDonald
